ut.title: Ultrasonic Testing & UT Inspection in Los Angeles, CA
ut.description: Ultrasonic thickness testing and UT weld inspection for Los Angeles refineries, harbor terminals, plants and steel structures. Request a UT quote today.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Inspection in Los Angeles, California
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT performs ultrasonic testing in Los Angeles: thickness surveys on piping, vessels and tanks, plate lamination checks, and angle-beam examination of structural and pressure-boundary welds. Technicians travel to your site in the harbor area, the South Bay, the San Fernando Valley or downtown, work to a written procedure, and return thickness grids and weld records that an inspector or engineer can act on. Send us the component, material, wall range and governing code and we reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Los Angeles

Los Angeles is two industrial economies stacked on one basin. Along the coast, the San Pedro Bay harbor complex moves a large share of the country's containerized trade; the Port of Los Angeles alone lists dozens of ship-to-shore container cranes across its terminals. Those cranes, their rail girders, the wharf steel and the bulk-liquid piping behind the terminals are all inspected for wall loss and weld integrity on a recurring cycle, and ultrasonic testing is the method that gives a number rather than an opinion.

Inland from the water sits the older process base: refining and storage in the harbor and South Bay districts, tank farms around Carson and Wilmington, and the pipeline rights-of-way that tie them together. The picture is changing, because refining in the basin is consolidating and some units have been announced for closure. For the equipment that stays in service, remaining-life questions become sharper, and a clean thickness history at fixed locations becomes the evidence that a vessel or line can keep running to its next planned outage.

The third pillar is construction. Downtown and Hollywood towers, hospital campuses, transit extensions and warehouse buildings in the Inland Empire corridor all use welded structural steel. Los Angeles is also the city that lives with the memory of the 1994 Northridge earthquake, when welded beam-to-column joints in steel moment frames cracked, and that history is why complete-joint-penetration welds in seismic frames are examined volumetrically rather than by eye alone.

What UT finds and what it misses

Ultrasonic testing sends a sound pulse into the part through a couplant and listens for what comes back. For thickness work, the time between the front-wall echo and the back-wall echo, multiplied by the velocity of sound in that material, gives remaining wall. For welds, an angled beam travels through the weld volume and reflects from planar flaws such as lack of fusion, incomplete penetration and cracks, which makes UT the practical volumetric method on thick sections.

It has limits that matter on Los Angeles assets. Heavy scale and bubbled coatings on harbor-side steel scatter sound and can give false readings unless the surface is dressed. Corrosion pits narrower than the probe face can be stepped over, so a spot reading may overstate the wall around a pit. Coarse-grained cast material and austenitic stainless welds attenuate the beam and need a modified technique. A thin or heavily laminated plate can produce a back-wall echo that is not the true back wall at all.

Because UT interprets reflections, it also depends on the person at the probe. That is why the procedure, the calibration blocks and the technician's qualification are written into the report and not left to memory.

Thickness surveys on piping, vessels and tanks

A corrosion-monitoring program is a set of condition monitoring locations, each with a defined spot or grid, read again at each campaign so the trend is comparable. Atlantis technicians use dual-element probes on corroded external surfaces, because the split transmit and receive crystals handle rough walls and pitted metal better than a single-crystal probe. Calibration is done on a step block of the same acoustic material across the range being read, and the A-scan display is watched so a doubled echo on thin wall or a laminar reflection is recognized instead of being logged as a good number.

Hot lines are common in refineries and process plants. High-temperature probes and couplants allow readings on lines that are still in service, and a temperature correction is applied to the velocity because sound slows as steel gets hotter. Where insulation has to be opened, the insulation contractor, the scaffold crew and the inspector are coordinated so the same opening serves every task. The governing practice for contact pulse-echo thickness gauging is ASTM E797, and ASME Section V Article 23 carries SE-797 for code work; our guide to the thickness-measurement requirements explains how the pieces fit.

The output feeds the owner's inspection program. Under API 510 for pressure vessels, API 570 for piping and API 653 for aboveground tanks, the owner's authorized inspector is responsible for the inspection and the remaining-life decision. Atlantis performs the examination and reports the readings; it does not act as the inspector of record.

Angle-beam examination of welds

Weld examination uses shear-wave probes at fixed refracted angles, commonly 45, 60 and 70 degrees, chosen so the beam meets the likely flaw orientation for the joint geometry. The technician builds a reference level or a distance-amplitude curve from side-drilled holes in a basic calibration block, sets scanning gain above reference, and scans from both sides of the weld where access allows. Indications are located by sound path and surface distance, sized against the curve or the code's method, and judged against the acceptance table that the code names.

For structural steel the working document is usually AWS D1.1, whose inspection clause includes ultrasonic examination of groove welds and its own acceptance classes by joint type and loading. Seismic force-resisting systems add the requirements of AISC 341 and AWS D1.8, the seismic supplement to D1.1. For bridge steel the document is AWS D1.5. For process piping and vessels the construction code supplies the criteria: ASME B31.3, with its examination table, or ASME Section VIII Division 1, whose Appendix 12 covers ultrasonic examination of welds. Atlantis does not decide which code applies; the engineer of record does, and the procedure is written to that choice.

Where an owner wants UT in place of a different volumetric method, the substitution has to be agreed with the owner, the engineer and any authorized inspector before work starts, because not every code permits it for every joint.

Codes, jurisdictions and acceptance in California

ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code Section V sets how UT is performed: Article 4 for welds, Article 5 for materials and Article 23 for the thickness practice. The construction code then sets what is acceptable. In California, the state's Division of Occupational Safety and Health runs a Pressure Vessel Unit under Labor Code sections 7620 to 7771, with unfired pressure vessel rules in Title 8, sections 450 to 560 and boiler rules in sections 750 to 797. The unit issues operating permits for items such as air tanks over 1.5 cubic feet and LP-gas storage over 125 gallons of water capacity, and the permit inspection is done by a state inspector or by a qualified inspector employed by an insurance company.

Inside the City of Los Angeles, the Department of Building and Safety handles permits for those items itself and registers deputy inspectors, including deputy pressure vessel inspectors. Process plants also fall under OSHA's process safety management rule, 29 CFR 1910.119(j), which requires inspection and testing of process equipment to recognized and generally accepted good engineering practice, and California adds its own enforcement and refinery-specific safety rules. UT data is one of the records those programs rely on.

Who does the work and under what authority

Atlantis technicians are qualified under the company's written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician sets up and calibrates the instrument, performs the examination and interprets the results. An ASNT NDT Level III approves the technique and the procedure and reviews reports. Anoop Rayavarapu, the founder and an ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, signs off the technique. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies its own personnel, so each report names the employer's qualification record for the technician rather than a card issued by an outside body.

Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. That covers the company's quality and environmental management systems; it is not a statement about any one examination, which stands on its procedure, calibration and qualification records.

The delivery model is straightforward. Atlantis has no office in Los Angeles. Technicians are mobilized to the site for the agreed scope, with equipment, blocks and procedure in hand, and travel is part of the quotation instead of a surprise.

What the Los Angeles UT report contains

  • Component identification, drawing or line number, material and nominal wall.
  • Procedure number and revision, with the code and edition it was written to.
  • Instrument, probe, couplant and calibration block identification, with calibration status on the day.
  • Technician name, method, level and the Level III who approved the technique.
  • For thickness work, a grid or table by condition monitoring location, minimum and average readings, and a sketch showing where each was taken.
  • For weld work, each indication with location, length, amplitude or size, and an accept or reject disposition against the named criteria.
  • Surface condition notes, access limits and any area not examined, stated plainly.

Raw data and sketches are kept so the next campaign repeats the same locations and the trend means something.

Planning a UT job in Los Angeles

Site access is the first schedule driver. Refinery and terminal gates ask for safety orientation, identity checks and sometimes port credentials, and these have lead times that the crew cannot shorten. Plan for them when you request the quote. Traffic on the 110, 405 and 710 corridors affects shift starts at the harbor, so crews are scheduled around gate hours.

The climate helps and hurts. Mild winters rarely stop UT, but sun-baked steel in inland summers can run well above comfortable handling temperature, and high-temperature couplant or shaded setups may be needed. Salt air near the harbor corrodes unprotected blocks and cables, so equipment is kept dry and checked. Santa Ana winds blow grit that gets into couplant and onto scan surfaces, which is one more reason to dress and clean the surface just before scanning.

Turnarounds and wharf outages are planned months ahead. If you are building scope for one, send thickness history and piping isometrics early, so the survey can be laid out before crews arrive.

UT, MT or PT for your Los Angeles job

Pick by the question. If the question is wall loss or a flaw inside a weld, UT is the tool. If the question is a surface crack in carbon or low-alloy steel, magnetic particle testing in Los Angeles is quicker and more sensitive at the surface. If the material is stainless, aluminum or any non-magnetic alloy, or the part is a casting or machined detail, liquid penetrant testing in Los Angeles finds the surface-breaking flaw. Many jobs use two: UT for thickness, MT or PT for cracking on the same weld.

For a broader view of the method, see our national ultrasonic testing service page and the complete UT guide. Statewide coverage is on the California inspection services page.

Training your own UT technicians

If you would rather build in-house capability, Atlantis runs UT Level 1 and UT Level 2 courses under SNT-TC-1A, and teams can practice on the UT simulator before hands-on work at the employer's facility. Our Los Angeles training page explains how the courses and the employer's written practice fit together, and written practice development is available if you need to set one up.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Los Angeles?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Los Angeles. Technicians are mobilized to your refinery, terminal, plant or construction site for the agreed scope, and travel is built into the quotation rather than added later.

faq.q: What can ultrasonic testing measure on piping and vessels in Los Angeles?
faq.a: Contact UT gives remaining wall thickness at defined condition monitoring locations. Repeated readings at the same spots show corrosion rate, which the owner inspection program uses for remaining-life and next-inspection decisions.

faq.q: Can UT be done on hot lines that are still running?
faq.a: Often yes. High-temperature probes and couplants allow readings on in-service lines, and a temperature correction is applied to the sound velocity. Surface temperature limits and site safety rules decide whether it is practical.

faq.q: Which code governs UT of structural steel welds?
faq.a: For buildings and general structures it is usually AWS D1.1, with AWS D1.8 added for seismic force-resisting systems. State bridge steel uses AWS D1.5. The engineer of record names the code, and the UT procedure is written to it.

faq.q: Does Atlantis act as the API inspector on a vessel or tank?
faq.a: No. Under API 510, 570 and 653 the owner authorized inspector remains responsible for the inspection. Atlantis performs the ultrasonic examination and reports the thickness data and indications for that inspector to use.

faq.q: What surface preparation does UT need?
faq.a: The surface must be free of loose scale, flaking paint and weld spatter so the probe couples cleanly. Rough or heavily coated areas are dressed locally, and the report notes any area that could not be prepared adequately.

faq.q: Can UT replace radiography on a weld?
faq.a: That depends on the construction code and the owner. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, so the substitution is agreed with the owner, engineer and authorized inspector before the work is planned.

faq.q: What do I get at the end of a UT job?
faq.a: A report with component identification, procedure and revision, equipment and calibration data, technician and level, thickness grids or weld indications, and an accept or reject disposition against the named criteria.

faq.q: How do I get a quote for UT in Los Angeles?
faq.a: Start with the quote link in the opening paragraph. Send the component list, material, wall range, code and site access rules, and we reply within one business day with questions or a scope.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection in Los Angeles, CA | MT
mt.description: On-site magnetic particle inspection (MPI) for Los Angeles harbor cranes, refinery vessels, structural welds and fabrication. Request an MT quote today.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Los Angeles, California
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT carries out magnetic particle inspection in Los Angeles on ferromagnetic steel: weld toes and fillet welds, crane and wharf structure, vessel nozzle attachments, castings and forgings. Technicians are mobilized to your yard, plant or fabrication shop with yokes, wet and dry particles and the lighting needed to see a fine crack, and they report each indication against the code that applies. Describe the weld or component and the material and we reply within one business day.

Where mag particle testing earns its place in Los Angeles

Surface cracks are what end the life of steel in motion, and Los Angeles has a lot of steel in motion. The container terminals around San Pedro Bay run rail-mounted gantry cranes and ship-to-shore cranes whose boom hinges, trolley rails, sill beams and portal legs see cyclic loading every shift. Fatigue cracks start at weld toes and at geometric transitions, and the first stage of finding them is a clean surface and a magnetic field.

The refining and storage district adds a second set of targets. Wet hydrogen sulfide service makes surface-breaking cracking a credible damage mechanism on carbon steel vessel shells and heat-affected zones, so nozzle welds, skirt attachments and repair welds are examined with MT during outages, often after grit blasting. Tank shell-to-bottom joints and shell welds on aboveground storage tanks are also routine MT targets when a floor or shell repair has been made.

Fabrication is the third channel. Welded structural steel for towers, hospital frames and transit structures is examined at the shop and in the field, usually with a yoke on the final pass, on repairs after gouging, and on temporary attachment removals where a surface crack could start from a ground-out scar. Steel moment frames carry added scrutiny because the region's seismic design relies on welds that can yield rather than fracture.

What MT detects and what it misses

The method magnetizes the part and applies fine ferromagnetic particles. A crack or other surface discontinuity disturbs the flux, a small leakage field forms across the gap, and the particles gather there as a visible line. This works only on ferromagnetic material: carbon steel and most low-alloy steels. Austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, copper and nickel alloys are not magnetic enough, so those require penetrant methods instead.

MT finds surface-breaking and slightly subsurface flaws, with sensitivity falling quickly as depth increases. It does not measure depth, does not find deep internal flaws, and can be fooled in several ways. A thick coating reduces the field at the surface. A sharp change in section can create a non-relevant indication that looks like a crack. Rough weld ripple, scale and grease hold particles where no crack exists. A good technician learns to tell relevant from non-relevant indications and, when in doubt, cleans and repeats the test.

Field direction matters. A crack is found best when the flux runs across it, which is why the procedure calls for two examinations at roughly right angles, so cracks in any orientation are covered.

Technique: yokes, particles and light

Most field MT on welds uses an electromagnetic yoke. An AC yoke is checked to confirm it can lift at least 10 pounds at the largest pole spacing used, and a DC or permanent-magnet yoke at least 40 pounds, as ASME Section V Article 7 requires. The technician places the legs across the weld, sweeps the surface, applies particles while the field is on, and repeats at a perpendicular orientation. Visible dry powder suits rough or warm surfaces; contrasting paint with black wet particles suits smoother steel.

Fluorescent wet particles are used where the highest sensitivity is needed. These are viewed under UV-A light in a darkened area, and the procedure sets the minimum light intensity at the surface and the maximum ambient white light. On open harbor wharves or in sunlit yards that means a tent or dark enclosure and a check with a calibrated light meter, because fluorescent examination in daylight simply does not work.

Where prods or coils or a stationary bench unit are used, the procedure sets current or field strength by part thickness and geometry and requires a field-strength check, often with a pie gauge or a shim indicator. Demagnetization follows when residual magnetism would interfere with later welding, with instruments, or with the part's service. Our complete MT guide walks through those choices step by step.

Codes and acceptance criteria that apply

ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code Section V, Article 7, controls how the examination is done. Acceptance comes from the construction code. For pressure vessels, ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6 covers magnetic particle methods and acceptance. For process piping, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.3 sets the method and Table 341.3.2 sets acceptance. For structural steel it is AWS D1.1, and for bridges AWS D1.5. ASTM E709 is the guide to the method and ASTM E1444 is the practice most specifications call out. Our Article 7 explainer covers the requirements in plain terms.

Atlantis does not choose among those documents. The engineer of record, the owner's specification or the authorized inspector does that, and the Atlantis procedure is written to match, with the edition recorded in the report.

California regulators care about the equipment you run. The state Division of Occupational Safety and Health enforces pressure vessel rules in Title 8 and operates a Pressure Vessel Unit, while the City of Los Angeles Department of Building and Safety handles permits and deputy inspector registration for items inside city limits. MT records can support the owner's file when a repair or alteration must be documented, and work on process equipment sits under OSHA process safety management, 29 CFR 1910.119(j).

Who performs and approves the examination

MT is performed by technicians qualified under the Atlantis written practice, which is based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II sets up the equipment, applies the technique and interprets and evaluates indications. An ASNT NDT Level III approves the procedure and reviews reports. Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, is the founder who approves the technique. The employer, not an outside body, certifies its personnel under SNT-TC-1A, so the qualification record that backs each report belongs to the employer.

Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001, which describe how the company manages quality and environmental impact. The examination itself is backed by the procedure, equipment checks and personnel qualification records described on this page.

Atlantis has no office in Los Angeles. Technicians travel to your site with their equipment for the agreed scope, and mobilization is quoted alongside the inspection so the full cost picture is clear before you approve.

What an MT report records

  • Component or weld identification, drawing reference and material specification.
  • Procedure number, revision, governing code and edition.
  • Equipment: yoke or bench unit, particle type and lot, carrier, light meters and the date of the last check.
  • Surface condition and preparation method, and the temperature of the part where it matters.
  • Technician, method and level, with the approving Level III.
  • Each indication with location, orientation and length, a photograph or sketch, and its disposition against the named acceptance criteria.
  • Whether demagnetization was done and how residual field was checked.

Photographs and a sketch are kept with the record so a repair can be tied to the indication that caused it.

Planning an MT job in Los Angeles

Surface condition decides how fast the work goes. Paint, rust and weld spatter have to come off before particles are applied, so coordinate with the blasting or grinding crew. At harbor terminals, work windows depend on vessel schedules and crane availability, and some cranes can be examined only when parked and locked out. Ask early about access equipment such as lifts or rope-free scaffolding for boom steel.

Temperature rarely limits MT in a mild coastal climate, but heat in inland summers matters. Steel in direct sun can be too hot for certain wet carriers, in which case dry powder or a shaded work window is the answer. Light is the second constraint. Fluorescent work in the open requires an enclosure, and daylight on sunny afternoons can overwhelm a yoke-and-UV setup unless a tent is built.

Refinery and terminal sites need orientation, gate time and hot-work or confined-space permits, and each adds lead time. Send your safety requirements with the quote request and we will plan around them.

What happens after an indication is found

An indication is not automatically a defect. The technician first decides whether it is relevant: a true discontinuity, rather than a particle trap at a weld ripple or a change in section. Relevant indications are measured and compared with the acceptance table. Linear indications are usually judged by length, rounded indications by diameter and spacing, and the code states how many may be present in a given area.

When an indication is rejectable, the usual path is to mark it, grind to remove it, re-examine the ground area to confirm the crack is gone, and weld-repair only if the remaining thickness requires it. The re-examination is recorded under the original report so the repair history stays attached to the weld. On pressure equipment, repairs and alterations follow the National Board Inspection Code or the owner's repair procedure, and the owner's inspector decides how they are documented. Atlantis reports the finding; the repair decision belongs to the engineer or authorized inspector.

On crane and terminal steel, an accepted crack-like indication may still be monitored. If the owner and engineer choose to keep a component in service with a known small flaw, the next examination should repeat the same location with the same technique, and the first report's sketch makes that possible.

MT, PT or UT for your Los Angeles inspection

If the steel is magnetic and the concern is a surface crack, MT is usually the fastest and most sensitive field choice. If the metal is stainless, aluminum or another non-magnetic alloy, switch to penetrant testing in Los Angeles. If you need wall thickness or have to look inside a weld, use ultrasonic testing in Los Angeles. Most structural and pressure-boundary jobs combine two. Our national magnetic particle testing page and the MT versus PT comparison help with the choice, and the California inspection services page shows how this fits with other work.

Building an in-house MT capability

If you want your own technicians qualified, Atlantis offers MT Level 1 and MT Level 2 training, with theory online and practical work at the employer's facility under a written practice. The Los Angeles training page explains the arrangement, and the SNT-TC-1A eligibility checker helps candidates see what hours and records they will need.

faq.q: What materials can magnetic particle inspection be used on?
faq.a: Only ferromagnetic materials, mainly carbon and low-alloy steels. Austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, copper and most nickel alloys are not magnetic enough, so liquid penetrant testing is used on them instead.

faq.q: How deep can MT find a crack?
faq.a: MT is strongest on flaws open to the surface and works slightly below it. Sensitivity falls quickly with depth, so it is not used to find deeper internal flaws, which is a job for ultrasonic testing.

faq.q: Do you perform MT through paint or coating?
faq.a: Thin, tightly bonded coatings may be acceptable if the procedure has been demonstrated for that thickness. Thicker coatings, scale or rust normally have to be removed because they weaken the field and hide indications.

faq.q: Why does MT need two examinations at right angles?
faq.a: A crack shows up best when magnetic flux runs across it. Examining twice at roughly right angles makes sure cracks in any orientation are caught, which is a requirement in ASME Section V Article 7.

faq.q: What is the difference between wet fluorescent and dry powder MT?
faq.a: Wet fluorescent particles give the highest sensitivity and need UV-A light in a darkened area. Dry powder is simpler on rough or warm surfaces. The procedure and acceptance criteria decide which is used.

faq.q: Is demagnetization always required after MT?
faq.a: No. It is done when residual magnetism could interfere with later welding, machining, instruments or service. The procedure states when it is needed and how the residual field is checked.

faq.q: Can MT be used on crane steel at the Los Angeles harbor?
faq.a: Yes, on ferromagnetic structure such as boom hinges, sill beams, rail attachments and weld toes. Work is scheduled around vessel and crane availability, lockout rules and the terminal safety requirements.

faq.q: Does Atlantis keep a crew stationed in Los Angeles?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Los Angeles. Technicians are mobilized from outside the city to your site for the agreed scope, and mobilization is shown in the quotation.

faq.q: How do I request an MT quotation?
faq.a: The contact form or the quote link at the top both work. Give the material, weld or component list, surface condition, code and access rules, and we reply within one business day.

pt.title: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in Los Angeles, CA
pt.description: Liquid penetrant testing and dye penetrant inspection for stainless, aluminum and alloy welds and castings across Los Angeles. Request a PT quote today.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Los Angeles, California
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT provides liquid penetrant testing in Los Angeles for the metals that magnetic particle inspection cannot handle: stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys, bronze and other non-magnetic material, along with carbon steel where a penetrant is the better fit. Technicians travel to your plant, shipyard or shop with penetrant systems, cleaners and developers, and report every surface-breaking indication against the code. Send the material, component and acceptance code and we reply within one business day.

Where penetrant testing is used around Los Angeles

Los Angeles has a large share of non-ferrous and stainless work for a US city. Along San Pedro Bay, ship repair yards handle aluminum superstructure, stainless piping and tanks, and bronze or nickel-aluminum-bronze propellers and rudder fittings, none of which respond to a magnet. Dye penetrant fits those repairs because it works on any clean, non-porous surface regardless of alloy.

In the process plants of the harbor and South Bay districts, austenitic stainless and duplex piping, weld overlay and clad surfaces on vessels, and small-bore alloy connections are routine penetrant targets. Fabrication shops across the basin build stainless process skids and food or beverage equipment where weld surfaces must be crack-free and finish-ground, and penetrant is the accepted check on each pass or final surface.

Machined and cast parts also come through: pump casings, valve bodies, hydraulic components and mounting hardware, where a surface crack from grinding, heat treatment or fatigue can be fatal to the part. Because the method does not depend on part geometry, it serves just as well on a threaded fitting as on a long weld.

What penetrant testing finds and what it misses

Penetrant testing finds only flaws that are open to the surface. Liquid is drawn into the crack by capillary action, the excess is removed, and a developer draws the trapped liquid back out so the crack shows as a bright or colored line. That is the entire mechanism, and it sets the limits.

A flaw that does not break the surface is invisible to PT, however large. A crack that has been smeared closed by grinding, peening or blasting can fail to take up penetrant, which is why cleaning and etching sometimes matter more than the penetrant itself. Porous materials absorb penetrant everywhere and give a meaningless background. Dirt, paint, oil, scale and water in the crack mouth block entry.

The method also gives no depth. A tight fatigue crack and a deep one can look the same at the surface. Where depth or sizing matters, a surface indication from PT may be followed by grinding to check depth or by ultrasonic examination of the weld, and the plan for that follow-up is better set before the job than after the indication appears.

Technique: from cleaning to final inspection

Every job starts with cleaning. The surface is scrubbed, degreased and dried so that nothing sits in a crack mouth. Where grinding or blasting has smeared metal over defects, a light etch may be used. The procedure names which cleaners are allowed, and for stainless and nickel alloys it controls halogen and sulfur content in the penetrant materials so they do not harm the alloy. Air-quality rules in the South Coast district also restrict volatile solvent use, so the choice of cleaners and removers is checked against site and district requirements.

Penetrant is then applied and allowed to dwell, the time depending on material, flaw type and temperature. Excess is removed by the method that the procedure specifies: water washable, post-emulsifiable, solvent removable or hydrophilic, all within the families covered by ASTM E165 and ASTM E1417. Developer is applied thinly and evenly, and the technician examines the surface after the developer time for indications, using good white light for visible dye or UV-A in a darkened area for fluorescent penetrant. The sensitivity level of the system is chosen for the job: a high-sensitivity fluorescent system for critical surfaces, a visible solvent-removable system for field welds.

The procedure has to be matched to the part. The standard range for the part and penetrant materials is 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit under ASME Section V Article 6; outside it, the procedure must be qualified for that temperature. On sun-heated stainless in a Los Angeles summer, that limit is easy to pass, and the answer is shade, waiting, or a qualified high-temperature procedure.

Codes and acceptance for Los Angeles work

ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code Section V, Article 6, is the method document. Acceptance comes from the construction code: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 for pressure vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 with Table 341.3.2 for process piping, AWS D1.1 and D1.6 where stainless structural welds apply, and the owner's specification for castings and machined parts. ASTM E165 is the practice for general industry. Our explainer on Article 6 requirements sets out the steps in plain language.

Atlantis follows the code that the engineer of record or owner names. We do not select it, and the report records the document and edition so the disposition can be traced.

In California, the state Division of Occupational Safety and Health regulates pressure vessels and boilers under Title 8, and the City of Los Angeles handles permits within city limits through its Department of Building and Safety. Owners of regulated equipment often use PT records in repair files, and plants covered by OSHA process safety management, 29 CFR 1910.119(j), rely on recognized good engineering practice for inspection and testing.

Who performs penetrant inspection and approves it

Technicians are qualified under the Atlantis written practice following ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II performs the test and interprets the result; an ASNT NDT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, is the founder behind the written procedures. Because SNT-TC-1A is employer-based, the employer certifies its own technicians and the qualification record backing the report is the employer's.

Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. Those standards govern management systems, and they sit alongside, not in place of, the procedure and personnel records that support each examination.

The delivery model is mobilization. Atlantis has no office in Los Angeles. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope with their own materials, and each batch of penetrant, cleaner and developer is recorded by lot so a report can be traced to what was used.

What a penetrant report contains

  • Part or weld identification, material and drawing reference.
  • Procedure number and revision, with the code and edition.
  • Penetrant type, method, sensitivity level, cleaner, remover and developer, by manufacturer and lot.
  • Surface preparation, part temperature, dwell time and developer time.
  • Technician, method and level, and the approving Level III.
  • Each indication by location, size and form (linear or rounded), with a photograph or sketch.
  • Accept or reject against the named criteria, and any area that could not be examined.

Where a rejectable indication is repaired by grinding and welding, the re-examination is recorded in the same report series so the history of the weld stays together.

Planning a PT job in Los Angeles

Cleaning drives the schedule, so budget time for it. Heavy paint and scale have to be removed, and rough weld surfaces may need light grinding. At harbor yards and terminals, work windows follow vessel and crane schedules, and hot-work or confined-space permits can add lead time. On plant turnarounds, the penetrant crew has to work after blasting and before insulation or coating closes the surface, which is a narrow window.

Weather in the basin is usually friendly to PT, but not always. Coastal humidity and marine layer can keep surfaces damp in the morning, and dew will contaminate a cleaned surface. Inland summer heat pushes steel surfaces past the standard temperature range. Wind carries dust that sticks to wet developer, so shielding the work area helps. Plan early starts on hot days and keep the surface covered between cleaning and examination.

Send site orientation and permit requirements with the quote request and we will build them into the plan.

Handling indications and repeat examinations

Penetrant indications are read against the acceptance table after the developer time, and the technician must judge them quickly because bleed-out spreads and can merge adjacent indications. Linear indications, those longer than three times their width, are treated differently from rounded ones, and the code sets the limits for each. False indications from rough surface texture, residual cleaner or a poorly removed excess are sorted out by cleaning the area again and repeating the whole process rather than by wiping and re-developing.

After a rejectable indication is ground out, the area is re-cleaned, re-examined and recorded. If grinding has smeared metal, a light etch before the repeat test is usually specified, because a tight crack can be closed over by a grinding wheel and then fail to take penetrant. Where a rejected weld is to be rewelded, the new weld is examined to the same code as the original.

For stainless equipment going into clean or corrosive service, owners often require that penetrant residues are removed completely after testing. The procedure then includes a post-cleaning step and, if needed, a check that the cleaner has not left a film behind. Atlantis records that step, since an incomplete cleanup can matter more to a stainless surface than the inspection itself.

PT, MT or UT for your Los Angeles job

PT is the method for non-magnetic alloys and for surface cracks in any non-porous material. On carbon steel, magnetic particle testing in Los Angeles is quicker and finds slightly subsurface flaws as well. For wall loss and internal weld flaws, ultrasonic testing in Los Angeles is the right tool. A common sequence is UT for the weld volume and PT for the final surface. See the national penetrant testing service page and our MT versus PT comparison for more, and the California inspection services page for related work.

Training technicians in penetrant testing

Teams that want their own PT technicians can use Atlantis PT Level 1 and PT Level 2 courses, with theory online and practical work at the employer's facility under its written practice. The penetrant testing simulator lets candidates rehearse the process steps, and the Los Angeles training page explains how it all fits together.

faq.q: What is the difference between dye penetrant and fluorescent penetrant?
faq.a: Visible dye penetrant shows as colored lines in white light and suits field work. Fluorescent penetrant glows under UV-A light in a darkened area and offers higher sensitivity for critical surfaces. The procedure selects one.

faq.q: Can penetrant testing find cracks below the surface?
faq.a: No. PT detects only discontinuities that are open to the surface. A flaw that does not reach the surface, however large, will not show, and ultrasonic testing is the usual method for internal flaws.

faq.q: Does PT work on stainless steel and aluminum?
faq.a: Yes. Penetrant works on any clean, non-porous material, which is why it is the main surface method for stainless, aluminum and nickel alloys. Penetrant materials are controlled for halogen and sulfur content on stainless and nickel alloys.

faq.q: What temperature limits apply to penetrant testing?
faq.a: The usual window in Article 6 of ASME Section V runs from 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for both the part and the penetrant materials. Beyond it, the procedure has to be qualified for the temperature actually used.

faq.q: Why does surface cleaning matter so much for PT?
faq.a: Oil, paint, scale, water and smeared metal block the crack mouth so penetrant cannot enter. Poor cleaning is the most common reason a real crack is missed, and the report notes how the surface was prepared.

faq.q: Can PT be done on a hot summer day in Los Angeles?
faq.a: Only if the part stays within the procedure temperature range or the procedure is qualified for higher temperature. Shade, early starts or waiting for the surface to cool are the usual ways to stay in range.

faq.q: Which code sets PT acceptance for pressure vessels and piping?
faq.a: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 applies to pressure vessels, and ASME B31.3 with Table 341.3.2 applies to process piping. The owner or engineer names the code and Atlantis writes the procedure to match.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Los Angeles?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Los Angeles. Technicians are mobilized to your site with materials and procedure for the agreed scope, and the quotation includes mobilization.

faq.q: How do I request a penetrant testing quote?
faq.a: The form on our contact page and the quote link in the first paragraph both reach us. Send the material, component list, surface condition, acceptance code and site access rules, and we reply within one business day.

rt.title: Radiography Alternatives in Los Angeles, CA | UT & Review
rt.description: Atlantis does not perform radiography in the US. For Los Angeles weld questions, UT is offered where codes allow it, along with Level III radiograph review.
rt.h1: Radiographic Testing (RT) Alternatives in Los Angeles, California
rt.html:
In Los Angeles, as in the rest of the country, Atlantis does not perform radiographic testing. Industrial radiography is a licensed activity: it falls under the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's rules in 10 CFR Part 34, or the equivalent rules of an Agreement State, and California is an Agreement State, so its own radiation control program licenses the work. The United States is simply outside what we offer for this method. If you searched for RT in Los Angeles, this page explains what we can do for the same weld-quality question.

Ultrasonic testing as a volumetric alternative

For many welds, the question radiography answers is whether there is a planar or volumetric flaw inside the joint. Ultrasonic examination with angle beams can answer the same question on thicker sections, and it needs no radiation exclusion zone, which is a practical advantage on busy harbor sites, refinery units and multi-trade construction floors. Our ultrasonic testing page for Los Angeles describes the technique, the equipment and the report.

Whether UT may replace RT on a particular joint is a code and contract question, not ours to settle. ASME B31.3 and API 1104 contain provisions for ultrasonic examination of production welds, AWS D1.1 has its own ultrasonic acceptance criteria for groove welds, and ASME Section VIII permits UT in place of radiography only under specific conditions. The substitution is agreed with the owner, the engineer of record and, for code work, the authorized inspector before the job is planned. Where the answer is no, the radiography has to be done by a licensed contractor, and we do not recommend or name one.

Where it is yes, a UT procedure is written to the code, the technician is qualified under the company's written practice following ASNT SNT-TC-1A, and the report records every indication and its disposition. Technicians are mobilized to your site, since Atlantis has no office in Los Angeles.

ASNT Level III radiograph review that needs no radiation licence

Reading a radiograph is separate from making one, and the review work needs no source and no licence. Atlantis can arrange an independent ASNT Level III review of film or digital images and the technique sheets that go with them, measured against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code. Typical requests are a second read on a disputed indication, a check that image quality indicators, density and coverage meet the technique, and a review of an RT contractor's procedure and written practice.

The founder, Anoop Rayavarapu, is ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, and Level III review is how that qualification is used on radiography work. The review concerns the images and documents you supply; it is not a substitute for the contractor's own qualified interpretation, and it does not make Atlantis the radiographer of record.

Los Angeles owners often have a mix of fabrication shop radiographs, field welds on piping tie-ins, and records inherited with equipment. A Level III review can sort those into images that meet the technique, images that need re-shooting and images that are fine but mis-documented.

Radiography theory and training

If your team needs to understand radiography, Atlantis offers training in the theory and technique side. The radiographic testing Level 2 course covers principles, exposure technique, image quality and interpretation, delivered under an employer's written practice. Practical exposure with sources has to be done under the licence of the employer or a licensed training provider, and we do not hold or arrange one. Our Los Angeles training page explains how the courses and the employer's written practice fit together, and the practice tests are a useful check before a certification exam.

Other conventional methods for Los Angeles

Atlantis also performs magnetic particle inspection and liquid penetrant testing in Los Angeles for surface-breaking flaws. Statewide scope is on the California inspection services page. To discuss a weld-examination question and how it can be answered without radiography, request a quote or ask for a Level III conversation through the Level III consulting page.

faq.q: Is radiographic testing available from Atlantis in Los Angeles?
faq.a: No. Industrial radiography requires a radiation licence, and Atlantis does not perform it in the United States, in Los Angeles or anywhere else in the country.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing replace radiography on my weld?
faq.a: Sometimes. ASME B31.3, API 1104 and AWS D1.1 contain ultrasonic provisions, and Section VIII allows it under conditions. The owner, engineer and authorized inspector must agree to the substitution before the job.

faq.q: Can Atlantis review radiographs taken by another contractor?
faq.a: Yes. An ASNT Level III can review film or digital images and technique sheets against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code, including a second read on disputed indications. No radiation licence is needed for review.

faq.q: Does Atlantis recommend a radiography contractor in Los Angeles?
faq.a: No. We do not recommend or name radiography contractors. If your code or contract requires radiography, choose a contractor licensed by the state radiation control program and qualified under your own requirements.

faq.q: Where can my team learn radiography theory?
faq.a: The radiographic testing Level 2 course covers principles, technique and interpretation under an employer written practice. Practical work with radiation sources must be done under a licence held by the employer or a licensed provider.
